hook: A baby monkey, given a choice between a wire figure that gives milk and a soft cloth figure that gives nothing, spends almost the whole day hugging the cloth one. That 1950s finding upended a common idea of why babies love their parents, and opened a lifetime of questions about how relationships grow.

figure.caption: Ecological systems theory: layers of influence around a child, all changing over time.

chain.cause: Warm, responsive care and comforting touch meet an infant’s needs
chain.effect: a secure attachment forms, and the child uses the caregiver as a base to explore

chain.cause: A child’s temperament and the parents’ style shape each other
chain.effect: warm, firm (authoritative) parenting is linked with better outcomes, though not as a simple cause

average health risks rise, while supportive relationships help many children do well

ideas: Ecological systems theory: a child develops inside nested layers (micro, meso, exo, macro), all changing over time (chrono).
Attachment grows from contact comfort and responsive care. In the strange situation, babies are secure, avoidant, anxious or disorganized; separation anxiety appears around 8 months.

Parenting styles: authoritative (warm and firm), authoritarian (strict, cold), permissive (warm, few limits). The links to outcomes are correlational and vary by culture; temperament shapes parenting too.

Erikson’s eight psychosocial stages run from trust versus mistrust to integrity versus despair. Teens explore identity status and possible selves; adults face the social clock and, in many countries, emerging adulthood.

misconception.wrong: Babies love their parents mainly because their parents feed them.
misconception.right: Harlow’s monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother that gave no milk. Comfort and responsive care, not food alone, build attachment.

summary: Social and emotional development happens inside nested systems, from family to culture. Attachment grows from contact comfort and responsive care and is classified as secure, avoidant, anxious or disorganized. Parenting styles and temperament shape each other. Erikson’s eight psychosocial stages, identity statuses, the imaginary audience and personal fable, emerging adulthood and the social clock mark later development, and adverse childhood experiences raise average risk without deciding any one life.
